case_study_insert.main_stem: Kestrel Ridge Footwear (KRF) is a public limited company in the footwear manufacturing sector, employing a workforce of 80. Founded in 2008 by Ravi Kestrel, the business supplies durable work boots to national retailers and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. KRF plans to invest $960,000 in an automated stitching line using recycled leather alternatives, financed by a $560,000 share issue and a $400,000 five-year bank loan. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 120,000 units a year. KRF faces a rising defect rate on stitching and growing labour turnover in its cutting room.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: The stitching line produced 30,000 boots last quarter with a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.8% a year ago. Customer returns fell from 55 to 26 per month. Average delivery lead time is 5.3 days. Market research with 700 trade buyers found that 58% would pay up to $1.20 more for boots made with recycled materials, and 46% check sustainability claims before ordering. A skills review shows 22 of 80 operatives lack training on the new stitching machines; college courses cost $1,100 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Kestrel Ridge Footwear for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has lifted the base interest rate from 4.25% to 5.0%, raising debt-servicing costs for variable-rate borrowers. (2) The national minimum wage will increase by 6.2% from $13.00 to $13.81 per hour from April 2026, pushing up wage costs. (3) Leather and synthetic upper input costs have risen 8.4% year-on-year, while consumer spending on footwear grew 2.1% in the same period.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for KRF of financing the stitching line with a share issue rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $560,000 share issue brings in equity that carries no interest or compulsory repayment, protecting KRF's cash flow while it carries $360,000 of fixed costs a year. With the base interest rate at 5.0%, a $400,000 bank loan would create an annual interest commitment; share capital instead lets the full $8.00 contribution on each boot remain available to absorb the 8.4% rise in upper-material costs without squeezing the $20.00 selling price to national retailers.

Point 2: Equity does not have to be secured against KRF's assets, so the automated stitching line cannot be repossessed if demand for work boots falls, which matters given the current 2.2% defect rate and labour turnover. As a public limited company, KRF can access a wide pool of investors for the $960,000 project without depending on one lender's conditions or covenants. The trade-off is dilution of existing shareholders, but for a large capital scheme this spreads risk more widely than concentrating it in a single bank loan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Consider print advertising in trade journals, sponsoring industry trade shows, or social media campaigns. Which should KRF choose to promote its recycled-material boots? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Print advertising in trade journals: Trade journals reach the 700 trade buyers who specify work boots, giving KRF a credible, targeted message about recycled leather. Costs are moderate and the message lasts, but print has no demonstration of boot durability and a long lead time, so it may not shift the 120,000-unit target quickly, and readership is shrinking.

Sponsoring industry trade shows: Trade shows let KRF display the boots, meet national retailers face to face and demonstrate stitching quality, which directly addresses buyer concerns behind the 2.2% defect rate. Sponsorship and stand costs are high and results depend on attendance; with 80 staff and a $400,000 loan, a single event can consume a large part of the promotional budget for only a few days of exposure.

Social media campaigns: Targeted campaigns can showcase the recycled-material story to the 58% of surveyed trade buyers who would pay $1.20 more and to the 46% who check sustainability claims, with measurable clicks at low cost per contact. Content can be updated fast and scaled nationally, though trade buyers may rely more on personal relationships and specifications than on social platforms.

Recommendation: KRF should choose social media campaigns, supported by small product samples sent to key retailers. They reach the exact sustainability-minded segment in the research, cost far less than a trade-show stand and travel further than print. Trade shows are rejected as expensive and short-lived for a business servicing a $400,000 loan; print is rejected as passive and unable to demonstrate the $1.20 recycled-material premium. Samples bridge the gap that social media cannot cover.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of KRF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of KRF with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade shows and print are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for KRF of using team working to reduce its stitching defect rate and labour turnover.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working gives the 80 operatives shared responsibility for a complete pair of boots, so problems in stitching are spotted and fixed by the people closest to the work. This can push the 2.2% defect rate down further and reduce the 26 monthly returns, because team members check each other's output rather than relying on distant inspection. It also suits the flat structure and democratic leadership already described in the case.

Point 2: Working in teams gives operatives social contact and a sense of belonging, which can raise morale in the cutting room where labour turnover is growing. Higher commitment reduces the need to recruit and train replacements at $1,100 per employee, protecting the 30,000 boots filled last quarter and the 120,000-unit annual target. Teams also spread skills, so the 22 operatives lacking training on the new stitching machines can learn from experienced colleagues while the automated line beds in, supporting Ravi Kestrel's expansion.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college for the 22 operatives. Which should KRF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching beside the new stitching machines is directly relevant to KRF's own equipment and quality standards, costs no fees and keeps the 22 operatives productive while they learn, protecting the 30,000 boots made last quarter and the improvement to a 2.2% defect rate. Its weaknesses are that mentor-operators lose production time, bad habits can spread, and there is no certificate if national retailers ask for evidence of competence.

Off-the-job training: A local college course at $1,100 per employee provides structured skills and a recognised qualification for all 22 staff, costing $24,200 in total — modest against the $960,000 investment. However, it removes 22 of 80 operatives from the line, cutting capacity when 120,000 boots are required, and generic content may not match KRF's stitching settings, so on-site follow-up would still be necessary.

Decision: KRF should choose on-the-job training first, adding short college modules for team leaders later. It is cheaper, machine-specific and avoids losing output while the defect rate and labour turnover are concerns; full off-the-job training is rejected because withdrawing 22 staff and spending $24,200 would disrupt retailer deliveries, and college qualifications can be layered on once the automated line is stable.

Additional considerations: With labour turnover growing in the cutting room, a recognised certificate from the $1,100 college course could help retain the 22 operatives and attract replacements, which on-the-job training alone cannot offer. KRF could stagger attendance so only a few of the 80 staff are away at once, protecting the 120,000-unit target while still gaining formal qualifications; this hybrid spreads the $24,200 cost without a sudden capacity loss.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to KRF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of KRF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of KRF with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how KRF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 120,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $360,000 fixed costs; loan and share-finance feasibility for the $960,000 line; and unit cost of $15.00 with productivity of 1,500 units per worker, used to tackle the 2.2% defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($20.00 − $12.00) = $360,000 ÷ $8.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20.00 − $12.00 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways KRF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 45,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 120,000 units, a margin of safety of 75,000 units, to justify the $960,000 stitching line.
2. Contribution of $8.00 lets managers test a retailer discount: a $1.20 concession leaves $6.80 per boot, showing the extra volume needed to cover $360,000 fixed costs.
3. Fixed costs and contribution set the volume required to service the $400,000 bank loan and justify the $560,000 share issue.
4. Unit cost of $360,000 ÷ 120,000 + $12.00 = $15.00 and productivity of 120,000 ÷ 80 = 1,500 units per worker allow weekly benchmarking and help target the 2.2% defect rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate KRF's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Which ratio provides the stronger evidence of improvement? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 35.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 22.5%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $1,800,000 = revenue $6,000,000 − cost of sales $4,200,000; $1,800,000 ÷ $6,000,000 = 30.0%. In 2025 gross profit of $2,520,000 = revenue $7,200,000 − cost of sales $4,680,000; $2,520,000 ÷ $7,200,000 = 35.0%. Operating profit rose from $720,000 to $1,080,000; $720,000 ÷ $6,000,000 = 12.0% and $1,080,000 ÷ $7,200,000 = 15.0%. Capital employed moved from $4,000,000 to $4,800,000; $720,000 ÷ $4,000,000 = 18.0% and $1,080,000 ÷ $4,800,000 = 22.5%. Interest payable was $120,000 then $150,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, so KRF's profitability strengthened. Gross profitability rose from 30.0% to 35.0%, consistent with better control of leather and stitching costs as the 2.2% defect rate fell. The operating return on sales improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, showing that the $360,000 fixed costs are being absorbed by higher output of 120,000 boots. Return on capital rose from 18.0% to 22.5% despite capital employed reaching $4,800,000, so the $960,000 line appears to be adding value rather than diluting returns.

Stronger evidence: the profit margin, because it improved by three percentage points straight from the given revenue and operating profit and is less distorted than returns measured against a growing capital base, which also reflects the $560,000 share issue.

Conclusion: KRF's financial performance has improved on every measure. The operating return on sales is the clearest indicator of efficiency, and although interest payable and the $400,000 loan remain commitments, the rising margins suggest the expansion is affordable.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements, and a justified conclusion naming the stronger evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for KRF of switching to recycled leather alternatives in its work boots.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled leather alternatives appeal to the 58% of 700 trade buyers who would pay $1.20 more, allowing KRF to protect its $8.00 contribution per unit while synthetic upper input costs rise 8.4%. The 46% who check sustainability claims also make the change a useful differentiator when bidding for national retailer contracts, supporting the $20.00 price point and the $960,000 stitching investment.

Disadvantage: Recycled materials may cost more or vary in quality, which would raise the $12.00 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the full $1.20 premium is secured across all buyers. Inconsistent material could also worsen the 2.2% stitching defect rate or shorten boot life, increasing the 26 monthly returns and risking retailer relationships just as KRF takes on a $400,000 loan to fund the new line. Losing a national retailer contract would threaten the 120,000-unit output that services both the loan and the $560,000 share issue's expectations of growth.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 5.0%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase and the 8.4% rise in leather and synthetic input costs will affect KRF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate (4.25% to 5.0%): If KRF's $400,000 five-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise costs 0.0075 × $400,000 = $3,000 a year. That is small next to $360,000 of fixed costs and disappears entirely if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates could still raise the cost of future borrowing and make retailers cautious about premium boots, but KRF can limit the risk by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage (6.2%, to $13.81 from $13.00 per hour): With a workforce of 80, including a cutting room with growing labour turnover, this rise feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so a total wage bill cannot be honestly calculated; the defensible test is productivity of 120,000 units ÷ 80 staff = 1,500 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is manageable; if it falls, unit labour costs rise and the $8.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (8.4% leather and synthetic uppers): The insert does not decompose the $12.00 variable cost, so only a bound is possible: if all of it rose 8.4%, that adds 8.4% × $12.00 = $1.01 per unit; across 120,000 boots that is about $121,200 a year (120,000 × $1.01). The $1.20 recycled-material premium can recover only part of this, while footwear spending grew just 2.1%.

Conclusion: The 8.4% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 120,000 boots and directly erodes the $8.00 contribution underpinning the $960,000 expansion. The interest effect is minor and fixable, and the wage rise can be offset if productivity holds, whereas input inflation attacks unit economics with little room to raise prices.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on KRF's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of KRF with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
